title: Play and Early Learning
summary: Play is a creative process in which a child uses mind and body free from externally imposed goals — a freely chosen engagement with objects, peers or oneself that allows exploring, experimenting and experiencing without threat. Piaget: responses repeated purely for functional pleasure; Froebel: highly serious and of deep significance. Definitions: Ross — joyful, spontaneous, creative activity in which man finds his fullest expression; Gross — instinctive practice of activities essential later in life; Stern — a free, self-contained activity driven by intrinsic motivation; Montessori — play is the work of the child; Hurlock — any activity directed to an end other than enjoyment is not play.

Physical: exercises the body, uses surplus energy, coordinates muscles. Social: friendships, cooperation, manners, solving problems with friends. Cognitive: observing, concentrating, experimenting, problem solving, vocabulary, imagination, creativity. Moral: right and wrong, respect for elders, behaviour with peers. Therapeutic: releases pent-up emotions; shy children open up, aggressive ones learn to wait, over-competitive ones accept losses. Recreational: enjoyment, relaxation, no boredom. Educational: colours, sizes, shapes and textures through toys. Research (Sergio Pellis) shows play changes neural connections in the front of the brain.

Piaget: practice play (sensorimotor stage, 0–2: repeated body movements, mouthing objects); symbolic play (2–7: an object stands for something else, make-believe and role play); games with rules (7–11: structured, social play). Smilansky: functional play (first stage — playing with objects, physical movements); constructive play (using objects to build something); dramatic play (using imagination); games with rules (competitive games accepting rules).

Parten's six social stages: unoccupied play (0–2, not really playing); solitary play (alone, common in young toddlers); onlooker play (watches others without joining, about 2½–3½ years); parallel play (side by side with similar toys, not together, about 2½–3½); associative play (3–4 years: play together but without a common goal or rules); cooperative play (organised groups, teamwork, leaders and roles, group goals).

First two years: sensorimotor play, play with objects (from 4–5 months, once eye-hand coordination allows grasping), symbolic play after the first year (a wooden block as a telephone), social play with adults from about 1½ years. Two to five years: play becomes purposeful; groups grow; playmates chosen by age and gender; solitary and parallel play; make-believe and dramatic play (shopkeeper, family roles). Five to twelve: systematic, logical, rule-bound competitive games such as football and basketball.

Materials must be attractive and accessible; open spaces allow free movement; adults should be present; mere display on shelves frustrates children. Points to keep in mind: ease of supervision, safety, space for free movement, children's interests, needs of the group and of each child, special activities placed handy, similar activities together, furniture of suitable size and height.

Indoor areas: dolls corner/dramatic area (role play with home objects); blocks or construction area (heavy blocks on low shelves; builds imagination, creativity, social and motor skills); library, books and puzzle area (well lit, low furniture); art area (near water); also discovery, music and movement corners. Toys: for physical movement, for constructive and creative play, and for dramatic and fantasy play, graded by age (birth–2: swings, large balls, pull-along toys; 2–4: blocks, picture books, puzzles, kitchen kits, drawing; 4–6: balance beams, water play, group games, slides and merry-go-rounds). Outdoor: tricycle paths, sand pit, water play, jungle gym, slides and swings, open green space; outdoor play needs supervision. Groups: large (circle time, stories, music), medium (10–12 children), small (fewer than six, for individual attention).

Cognitive and language: sense games, concept formation (colour, shape, size, number), puzzles, story and picture completion, memory games, sequencing, arranging objects by size, matching pictures, observing nature; for language — conversation, stories, role play, puppets, listening games. Affective: dramatising stories, singing, reciting poems in rhythm, dressing dolls, group celebrations. Psychomotor: gross — pushing, pulling, throwing, catching, pedalling, jumping, swinging; fine — stringing beads, printing, tearing, cutting, collage, clay. Thematic planning: themes from the child's environment (myself, family, food, water, seasons, people who help me) for a week or two.

Observer (watches interaction and use of materials to plan better play), facilitator (arranges equipment, lets children speak and ask questions), reviewer (checks whether play met each child's needs and the curriculum goals and informs parents) and organiser (prepares a safe, happy, challenging play environment and materials).

vsa: Describe and differentiate dramatic play and games with rules given by Smilansky.

Dramatic play: children use imagination to turn objects into something else and act out roles (shopkeeper, mother). Games with rules: competitive games in which children understand, accept and play by rules. Dramatic play is free and imaginative; games with rules are structured and come later.
Describe onlooker play with an example.

In onlooker play a child watches others play but does not join; the child may talk to them to learn about the game. It is common at about 2½–3½ years. Example: a child stands near children playing with blocks, watching and asking questions, without building.
Describe any two levels of play given by Piaget.

Any two: practice play (0–2 years, sensorimotor — repeated body movements, putting objects in the mouth, blowing spit bubbles); symbolic play (2–7 years — an object stands for something, make-believe and role play); games with rules (7–11 years — accepting rules, structured social play).
Discuss the physical and social values of play.

Physical: activates different parts of the body, uses surplus energy that would otherwise make children irritable, and coordinates muscles and purposeful movement. Social: children form friendships, learn cooperation, social manners and ways of solving problems with friends through maximum social contact.
Discuss the therapeutic and recreational values of play.

Therapeutic: play releases pent-up emotions — shy children enjoy being with others, aggressive ones learn to wait for their turn, over-competitive ones learn to accept loss, insecure ones gain self-respect. Recreational: play gives enjoyment and relaxation, keeps children emotionally satisfied and prevents boredom.
Play in which a child uses an object as a symbol of something else — for example, a wooden block as a telephone — and engages in make-believe and role play; Piaget placed it at 2–7 years.

sa: Play changes with biological, social, emotional and intellectual maturity. First two years: sensorimotor play with body movements, object play from 4–5 months, symbolic play after the first year, social play with adults from about 1½ years. Two to five: play becomes purposeful; groups grow and playmates are chosen by age and gender; solitary and parallel play; make-believe and dramatic play (shopkeeper, family). Five to twelve: play becomes systematic, logical and rule-dominated, with competitive games like football and basketball.
What factors should be considered in designing an environment conducive to play and early learning?

Ease of supervision and guidance; attention to safety; maximum space for free movement; children's interests; needs of the group and of each child; special activities placed where they are readily available; similar activities kept together; furniture and shelves of suitable size and height. Materials should be attractive and within children's reach, and adults should be present to interact.
Describe planning a play activity on the theme 'water'.

Plan for a week in line with children's age and interest. Cognitive: talk about uses and sources of water, sort things that float and sink, measure and pour water into containers of different sizes. Language: rhymes and stories about rain and rivers, picture talk. Creative: paint with water colours, make paper boats. Physical: water play in tubs, pouring and squeezing sponges. Social and health: discuss saving water and washing hands, take a walk to see a pond or tap.
What is meant by a thematic approach in planning play activities?

Play activities in all domains are planned around a theme from the children's environment — such as myself, family, food, water, clothes, seasons, people who help me — for a week or two. The theme suits the children's age and interest, builds on first-hand, concrete experiences and broadens ideas they are familiar with, instead of imposing knowledge subject by subject.

la: Explain the types of play in early years with examples.

Piaget: practice play (0–2, repeated movements, mouthing objects), symbolic play (2–7, block as a telephone, role play), games with rules (7–11, structured games). Smilansky: functional play (playing with objects, physical movement), constructive play (building towers with blocks), dramatic play (imaginative role play), games with rules (competitive games). Parten (social): unoccupied play (newborns, not engaged), solitary play (alone with different toys), onlooker play (watching others), parallel play (side by side with similar toys), associative play (3–4 years, together without common goals), cooperative play (organised groups with roles and group goals, e.g. a team game).

or: Describe any two activities for social development among children.

(1) Group games and play — e.g. passing the ball in a circle or a relay: children take turns, follow rules, cooperate and learn to accept losing. (2) Group celebrations — e.g. celebrating each child's birthday or a festival together: children share, help in arranging things, appreciate others and feel part of a group. Also cleaning the work place together and dramatising stories.

la: Explain the term 'play'. Suggest the steps you would take to identify equipment and materials for outdoor play for children of 4–6 years.

Play is a child's freely chosen, joyful, creative activity of mind and body without externally imposed goals; Montessori called it the work of the child. Steps: (1) observe the children's interests, abilities and needs, including those with disabilities; (2) list equipment for large-muscle activities — running, climbing, jumping, sliding, swinging, balancing: balance beams, slides, swings, merry-go-round, jungle gym, materials for group games (ball, bat), water play, sand pit, tricycles; (3) check safety, sturdiness, size and height, and enough pieces for the group; (4) plan the space — paths for tricycles, sand and water areas, fixed swings and slides, open green space — so supervision is easy; (5) prefer low-cost and local materials such as old tyres; (6) rearrange with the seasons and review use.

or: Describe play activities in the context of children. Discuss the role of the teacher in promoting children's play in a centre.

Play activities cover all domains: cognitive and language (puzzles, sorting, stories, role play), affective (dramatisation, songs, dressing dolls), psychomotor (throwing, jumping, threading beads, clay). Teacher's role: observer — watches how children interact and use materials, to plan better play; facilitator — arranges equipment and climate, lets children speak freely and encourages questions; reviewer — checks after each activity whether it met each child's needs and the curriculum goals, and informs parents; organiser — prepares a safe, happy, interesting and challenging indoor and outdoor play environment with suitable materials.
